blocks.text: A 31-year-old woman attends an antenatal clinic at approximately 10 weeks' gestation for a routine ultrasound. She feels well and has had no vaginal bleeding or abdominal pain.
Ultrasound demonstrates an intrauterine embryo without detectable cardiac activity.

items.text: Take a focused history.
Explain the ultrasound findings and establish whether pregnancy loss can be diagnosed.
Discuss investigations and differential diagnoses.
Explain expectant, medical and surgical management.
Counsel the patient about follow-up, complications and future fertility.

blocks.text: Missed miscarriage is a non-viable intrauterine pregnancy that has not been expelled from the uterus.
The patient may have no symptoms, or may report mild spotting, loss of pregnancy symptoms or a history of a previously identified fetal heartbeat that is no longer detectable.

items.text: Minimal or absent vaginal bleeding.
Little or no abdominal pain.
Cervical os usually closed.
Ultrasound shows an embryo or gestational sac meeting accepted criteria for pregnancy loss.
Pregnancy tissue remains within the uterus.

blocks.text: Critical OSCE point: An embryo without visible cardiac activity on a single early ultrasound does not always mean miscarriage. The diagnosis must meet validated ultrasound criteria or be confirmed by appropriately timed repeat imaging.

subsections.subsection_title: 3. Differentiate missed miscarriage from other types

rows: Persistent bleeding and cramps may occur

blocks.text: This station places particular emphasis on breaking bad news and supporting a patient who may have attended expecting reassurance.

items.text: Introduce yourself and confirm the patient's identity.
Ensure privacy and ask whether she would like a support person present.
Establish what she understands about the ultrasound so far.
Explain that you need to discuss the findings and what they may mean.
Use clear, sensitive language and pause to allow questions.
Avoid giving a definitive diagnosis until the ultrasound criteria have been met.
Offer emotional support and arrange time for the patient to process the information.

blocks.text: A useful opening statement when the diagnosis is not yet confirmed:

"The scan has raised a concern about how the pregnancy is developing. Sometimes an early scan cannot give us a definite answer, so I would like to review the measurements and findings carefully before explaining what they mean and whether another scan is needed."
If pregnancy loss is confirmed:

"I am very sorry, but the scan confirms that the pregnancy is no longer developing. I understand this may be upsetting. I would like to explain the findings, answer your questions and discuss the options available to you. You do not need to make every decision immediately if you are medically stable."
Avoid phrases such as "your body has rejected the baby" or "at least you can try again." These may sound blaming or dismissive.

Assess whether she wants information about future fertility, investigations after recurrent pregnancy loss or psychological support. Do not assume how she feels about the pregnancy.
The examination is often less diagnostically important than ultrasound in an asymptomatic patient with suspected missed miscarriage.

blocks.text: If indicated, assess for abdominal tenderness, guarding or other signs of an acute abdomen.
The abdomen may be entirely normal in missed miscarriage.
These are not routinely necessary in an asymptomatic patient with a definitive ultrasound diagnosis.
If bleeding or pain is present, examination may help identify the source of bleeding, cervical dilatation, tissue at the cervical os or signs of infection.
Exam tip: Do not perform an invasive examination simply to confirm what a definitive ultrasound has already established, unless there is a clinical indication.

content_groups.group_title: A. Transvaginal ultrasound — the key investigation

blocks.text: Transvaginal ultrasound is the preferred investigation for assessing early pregnancy viability.

items.text: Location of the gestational sac.
Presence of a yolk sac.
Presence and size of the embryo.
Crown-rump length (CRL).
Mean sac diameter (MSD).
Presence or absence of embryonic cardiac activity.
Any adnexal abnormality or pelvic free fluid if clinically indicated.

content_groups.group_title: B. Ultrasound criteria for diagnosing miscarriage

blocks.text: This is one of the most important examination areas because an incorrect diagnosis can lead to interruption of a potentially viable pregnancy.
Using conservative criteria commonly recommended in early pregnancy assessment:

rows: CRL of 7 mm or more with no detectable cardiac activity
Diagnostic criterion for pregnancy loss, subject to appropriate image quality and clinical protocol
MSD of 25 mm or more with no embryo
Diagnostic criterion for pregnancy loss, subject to appropriate image quality and clinical protocol
CRL below 7 mm without cardiac activity
MSD below 25 mm without an embryo
Uncertain measurements or poor image quality
Expert review and/or repeat scan required

blocks.text: When findings are below the diagnostic thresholds, repeat transvaginal ultrasound after an appropriate interval, commonly at least 7 days, may be needed. Depending on the initial findings and the applicable guideline, a longer interval may be necessary.

The time-based criteria also matter. For example, the absence of an embryo with cardiac activity at least 11 days after a scan showing a gestational sac with a yolk sac, or at least 14 days after a scan showing a gestational sac without a yolk sac, can support diagnosis of pregnancy loss under accepted consensus criteria.
Always follow the local guideline and obtain a second opinion when required. Do not diagnose miscarriage solely because the pregnancy appears smaller than expected for the LMP.
β-hCG may help when ultrasound findings remain uncertain or pregnancy location has not been established.

items.text: A single β-hCG value cannot diagnose missed miscarriage.
Serial β-hCG is not routinely required when a definitive non-viable intrauterine pregnancy has already been established.
If the pregnancy location is uncertain, ectopic pregnancy must remain in the differential diagnosis.

blocks.title: Depending on symptoms and the proposed management:

items.text: Full blood count if bleeding is significant or anaemia is suspected.
Blood group and RhD status according to the local protocol.
Group and save or crossmatch if significant bleeding or surgery is anticipated.
Renal and liver function when clinically indicated or before relevant medication.
Infection investigations if fever or other signs of infection are present.

blocks.text: Routine extensive investigations are not required for every first miscarriage. Investigations for recurrent pregnancy loss depend on the patient's history and the relevant guideline.
1. Missed miscarriage
A non-viable intrauterine pregnancy remains in the uterus, often with little or no bleeding.
2. Very early viable pregnancy
Cardiac activity or an embryo may not yet be visible because the pregnancy is earlier than expected.
3. Anembryonic pregnancy
A gestational sac develops without a visible embryo. Diagnosis requires accepted ultrasound criteria or appropriate repeat imaging.
4. Ectopic pregnancy
Consider if the pregnancy location has not been definitively established, particularly if pain or haemodynamic symptoms develop.
Once non-viability has been reliably confirmed, management depends on clinical stability, infection risk, bleeding, gestational age, patient preference and local guidance.

Medication is used to facilitate expulsion of pregnancy tissue.

A commonly recommended regimen for missed miscarriage is mifepristone 200 mg orally, followed approximately 48 hours later by misoprostol 800 micrograms, using the permitted route and protocol specified by the treating service.
Exact regimens and eligibility must follow current local guidance. Alternative regimens may be used when mifepristone is unavailable or unsuitable.

blocks.text: No single option is best for every patient. Shared decision-making is essential, provided the selected approach is clinically safe.
A missed miscarriage may be especially distressing because the patient can feel completely well and may not understand how the pregnancy could have stopped developing.
Use a compassionate, structured approach.

items.text: Prepare: ensure privacy and adequate time.
Assess understanding: ask what the patient has been told about the scan.
Explain clearly: use direct but sensitive language.
Pause: allow silence and emotional reactions.
Respond empathetically: acknowledge grief and uncertainty.
Explain options: discuss expectant, medical and surgical management.
Arrange support: provide written information, follow-up and access to emotional support.

blocks.text: Example explanation after confirmation:

"I am very sorry. The ultrasound has confirmed that the pregnancy has stopped developing. This is not something you should blame yourself for. I understand that this may be very upsetting, and we can take time to discuss what this means and the options available. You can ask me anything, and I will support you through the next steps."
Avoid falsely reassuring the patient that a future pregnancy is guaranteed, but explain that many women go on to have successful pregnancies after miscarriage.

items.text: Vaginal bleeding and haemorrhage.
Retained products of conception.
Infection and septic miscarriage.
Need for additional medical or surgical treatment.
Medication-related pain, bleeding and gastrointestinal effects.
Anaesthetic complications.
Uterine perforation or cervical injury during surgery.
Infection.
Intrauterine adhesions, which can occasionally affect menstruation or fertility.
Grief and sadness.
Anxiety about future pregnancies.
Feelings of guilt or self-blame.

blocks.text: Offer support according to the patient's needs and preferences.
Before discharge, ensure that the patient is clinically stable, understands her management plan and has access to emergency care.

items.text: Heavy or rapidly increasing vaginal bleeding.
Severe or worsening abdominal pain.
Fever or chills.
Offensive vaginal discharge.
Dizziness, fainting or collapse.
Marked weakness or feeling acutely unwell.

blocks.text: Follow-up depends on the management approach and local protocol. A home pregnancy test may be recommended at a defined interval, often around three weeks after expectant or medical management. A persistently positive test or ongoing symptoms requires reassessment.
If the initial ultrasound was inconclusive rather than diagnostic, repeat imaging must occur at the appropriate interval before a definitive diagnosis is made.
Explain that most women can conceive successfully after an uncomplicated miscarriage. Discuss future conception when the patient feels physically and emotionally ready.

If there is a history of recurrent pregnancy loss, offer appropriate assessment according to local guidelines. Investigations may include assessment for antiphospholipid syndrome, uterine abnormalities, thyroid disease and selected genetic causes, depending on the clinical history and guideline criteria.

subsections.subsection_title: 13. How to report your findings in the OSCE

blocks.text: "This is a woman at approximately 10 weeks' gestation who is clinically stable and has minimal or no vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates a non-viable intrauterine pregnancy meeting accepted diagnostic criteria for pregnancy loss. The findings are consistent with missed miscarriage. I would explain the diagnosis compassionately, assess for complications, and discuss expectant, medical and surgical management according to her preferences and clinical circumstances."

"The ultrasound demonstrates an intrauterine pregnancy without detectable cardiac activity, but the measurements do not meet definitive criteria for pregnancy loss. I would explain the uncertainty, arrange expert review and appropriately timed repeat transvaginal ultrasound, and avoid initiating treatment until the diagnosis is established."

content_groups.group_title: Example C: Missed miscarriage with suspected infection

blocks.text: "The patient has a confirmed non-viable intrauterine pregnancy with fever, uterine tenderness and systemic symptoms concerning for infection. I would initiate urgent sepsis assessment and treatment, commence appropriate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and arrange urgent senior gynaecological review for source control."

subsections.subsection_title: 14. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. Define missed miscarriage.
Answer: A non-viable intrauterine pregnancy that has not been expelled from the uterus.
Q2. Why may the patient have no symptoms?
Answer: The pregnancy may have stopped developing before the body initiates expulsion, so bleeding and pain may be absent or minimal.
Q3. What are the key ultrasound criteria?

Answer: A CRL of at least 7 mm without cardiac activity or an MSD of at least 25 mm without an embryo are commonly accepted diagnostic criteria on transvaginal ultrasound, subject to image quality and the applicable protocol. Smaller or equivocal findings require appropriately timed reassessment.
Q4. What are the management options?
Answer: Expectant management, medical management and surgical management. The choice depends on stability, complications, patient preferences and local guidance.
Q5. When is urgent intervention necessary?
Answer: Significant haemorrhage, haemodynamic instability, suspected infection requiring source control or another urgent clinical indication.
Q6. Is serial β-hCG always required?
Answer: No. It may be useful when pregnancy location or viability is uncertain, but it is not routinely necessary once a definitive non-viable intrauterine pregnancy has been established.
Q7. How would you counsel the patient about future fertility?
Answer: Explain that many women have successful future pregnancies after miscarriage, offer appropriate follow-up and address any history of recurrent pregnancy loss.
Q8. What is the most important diagnostic error to avoid?
Answer: Prematurely diagnosing miscarriage on an equivocal early ultrasound, potentially interrupting a viable pregnancy.

items.text: Diagnosing miscarriage from absent cardiac activity without checking the embryo's measurements and accepted criteria.
Using the LMP alone to determine whether a heartbeat should be visible.
Failing to distinguish confirmed pregnancy loss from uncertain viability.
Starting medical treatment before establishing the diagnosis.
Forgetting to discuss all three management options.
Failing to assess for haemorrhage or infection.
Giving insensitive or blaming explanations.
Omitting safety-net advice and follow-up.
Assuming one miscarriage automatically requires extensive investigations for recurrent pregnancy loss.
